title: Light Pollution
summary: How too much artificial light at night hides the stars, confuses animals like sea turtles and birds, disturbs sleep, and how it can be reduced.
poll: Cities should turn off or dim more of their lights at night.

versions.title: Where Did the Stars Go?
versions.text:
Go out at night in a big city. Look up. Can you see lots of stars? Most likely, you can not.

The sky is not dark. It glows from all the lights. Street lamps shine up. Signs shine up. Homes shine up, too. Too much light at night is called light pollution.

Light can make a mess for us. We can not see the stars. Kids in towns may not see the Milky Way. It is a band of stars.

Light can hurt wild things, too. Baby sea turtles hatch on the beach at night. They crawl to the bright sea. But a bright road can trick them. They go the wrong way.

Some birds fly at night. They use the stars to find their way. Bright lights can make them get lost. Bugs fly round and round lamps.

Too much light can make it hard for us to sleep. And lights left on waste power.

We can help! Point lamps down. Turn off lights we do not need. Then the stars can shine for all.

versions.title: Where Did the Stars Go?
versions.text:
Go outside at night in a big city. Look up. How many stars can you see? Most likely, just a few.

The sky over a city is not dark. It glows from all the lights below. Street lamps send light up. So do signs and homes. Too much light at night is called light pollution.

Light pollution hides the stars. Many kids in cities have never seen the Milky Way. It is a long band of stars across the sky.

Light pollution can hurt animals, too. Baby sea turtles hatch on the beach at night. They crawl toward the bright sea. But a bright road can trick them. They go the wrong way.

Some birds fly at night. They use the stars to find their way. Bright lights can make them lose their way. Bugs fly in circles around lamps.

Too much light at night can also make it hard for people to sleep. Lights left on waste power and money.

We can help! Point lamps down, not up. Turn off lights we do not need. Then the stars can shine for everyone.

versions.title: Too Much Light at Night
versions.text:
Go outside at night in a big city and look up. How many stars can you see? You may see only a few, even on a clear night.

The sky over a city is not truly dark. It glows from all the lights below. Street lamps, bright signs, and buildings all send light up into the sky. Too much light at night is called light pollution.

Light pollution hides the stars. Many children who live in cities have never seen the Milky Way, a long band of stars across the sky. In the desert, far from cities, the sky is still dark and full of stars.

Light pollution can harm animals, too. Baby sea turtles hatch on the beach at night. They crawl toward the brightest place, which is usually the sea. But bright lights on land can trick them, and they head the wrong way.

Some birds fly at night and use the stars to find their way. Bright lights can make them lose their way. Insects fly in circles around lamps.

Too much light at night can also make it hard for people to sleep. Lights left on waste power and money.

We can all help. Point lamps down, not up. Turn off lights we do not need. Then the stars can shine for everyone.

versions.text:

When there is too much artificial light at night, scientists call this problem light pollution.

As a result, many children who live in cities have never seen the Milky Way, the long band of stars that stretches across the sky. Far out in the desert, however, away from the glow of cities, the night sky is still dark and crowded with stars.

Many birds migrate at night, using the stars to guide them on their long journeys. Bright lights can confuse these birds and pull them off course, and some even crash into illuminated buildings. Insects also circle around lamps until they are too exhausted to fly.

Too much light at night can make it more difficult for people to sleep well, and lights that are left on for no reason waste energy and money.

Fortunately, light pollution is easy to reduce. We can shield lamps so that they shine downward instead of upward, and we can switch off lights that we do not need, so the stars can shine for everyone.

versions.title: Light Pollution: Losing the Night Sky
versions.text:
Step outside at night in a large city and look up, and you may notice that only a handful of stars are visible, even when the sky is completely cloudless.

The sky above a city is never truly dark, because it glows from the countless lights below. Street lamps, brilliant advertisements, and tall buildings send light upward into the atmosphere, where it spreads out and conceals the stars. When there is excessive artificial light at night, scientists call this problem light pollution.

As a result, many children who live in cities have never seen the Milky Way, the long band of stars that stretches across the sky. Far out in the desert, however, away from the glow of urban areas, the night sky is still dark and crowded with stars.

Light pollution can also harm wildlife. Baby sea turtles hatch on beaches at night, including beaches along the Red Sea, and they instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the sea. Bright lights on land can confuse them, so they wander toward roads instead of the water.

Many birds migrate at night, using the stars to guide them on their long journeys. Bright lights can confuse these travelers and pull them off course, and some even collide with illuminated buildings. Insects also circle around lamps until they are too exhausted to fly.

Excessive light at night can make it more difficult for people to sleep well, and lights that are left on unnecessarily waste electricity and money.

Fortunately, light pollution is relatively easy to reduce. Communities can shield lamps so that they shine downward instead of upward, and families can switch off lights that they do not need, so the stars can shine for everyone.

versions.title: Light Pollution
versions.text:
Step outside at night in a large city and look up, and you may notice that only a handful of stars are visible, even though thousands should be visible to the naked eye on a cloudless night.

The sky above a city is never truly dark, because a dome of light called skyglow hangs over it. Street lamps, brilliant advertisements, and towering buildings send light upward into the atmosphere, where it scatters and conceals the stars. When there is excessive artificial light at night, scientists call this problem light pollution.

As a result, many children who live in cities have never seen the Milky Way, the long band of stars that stretches across the sky, and researchers estimate that more than a third of all people on Earth can no longer see it from where they live. Far out in the desert, however, away from the glow of urban areas, the night sky is still dark and crowded with stars.

Light pollution can also harm nocturnal wildlife, meaning animals that are active at night. Baby sea turtles hatch on beaches at night, including beaches along the Red Sea, and they instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the sea. Bright lights on land can disorient them, so they wander toward roads instead of the water.

Many birds migrate at night, using the stars to guide them on their long journeys. Bright lights can disorient these travelers and pull them off course, and some even collide with illuminated buildings. Insects also circle continuously around lamps until they are too exhausted to fly.

Excessive light at night can disturb human sleep as well, because darkness signals the body to produce melatonin, a hormone that makes us sleepy. In addition, lights that are left on unnecessarily waste electricity and money.

Fortunately, light pollution is relatively easy to reduce. Communities can install shielded fixtures that direct light downward instead of upward, and families can switch off lights that they do not need, so the stars can shine for everyone.

versions.title: Light Pollution: Losing the Night Sky
versions.text:
Venture outdoors at night in a large city and look up, and you will probably discover that only a handful of stars are visible, even though thousands should be observable to the naked eye on a cloudless night far from any settlement.

The sky above a city is never genuinely dark, because a luminous dome called skyglow hangs over it. Street lamps, brilliant advertisements, and towering buildings send illumination upward into the atmosphere, where it scatters in every direction and conceals the stars. When there is excessive artificial light at night, scientists describe the problem as light pollution.

As a consequence, many children who live in cities have never observed the Milky Way, the luminous band of stars that stretches across the sky, and researchers estimate that more than a third of humanity can no longer see it from where they live. Far out in the desert, however, away from the glow of urban areas, the night sky remains dark and crowded with stars, and remote regions of Saudi Arabia offer exceptionally dark skies that attract astronomers and curious visitors alike.

Light pollution can also harm nocturnal wildlife, meaning animals that are primarily active at night. Newly hatched sea turtles emerge on beaches after dark, including beaches along the Red Sea, and they instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the moonlit sea, but artificial lights on land can disorient them, so they wander toward roads instead of the water.

Numerous bird species migrate at night, using the stars to navigate during their extensive journeys, but brilliant lights can disorient these travelers and pull them off course, and some even collide with illuminated buildings. Insects similarly circle around lamps until they are too exhausted to fly, which disrupts the delicate ecosystems that depend on them.

Excessive light at night can disturb human sleep as well, because darkness signals the body to produce melatonin, a hormone that makes us drowsy, and lights that are left on unnecessarily squander electricity and money.

Fortunately, light pollution is comparatively easy to reduce, because, unlike many other forms of pollution, it disappears the moment a light is switched off. Communities can install shielded fixtures that direct illumination downward instead of upward, and households can extinguish lights that are unnecessary, so that the stars can once again shine for everyone.
